verdict_reasoning: The connection-rate threshold has support in the thread, so the goal is not in question. The CPU-based log_postmaster_overloads is: message #7 asked to drop it, and v3 and v4 keep it without answering the misfire concern (standards-compat-1), the missing test (maintenance-fit-1) or the overlap with per-process OS monitoring (already-exists-1). The list needs to settle whether that GUC stays before code review makes sense. The duplicate lines and the GUC name are smaller, fixable points.

brief.title: Log postmaster overload and connection storms via two new GUCs
brief.problem: DBAs cannot tell afterwards how busy the postmaster was, because log_connections is too costly to keep on and pg_stat_database counters hold no history or CPU usage. A single postmaster at 100% CPU is easy to miss on large machines, so connection storms, slow fork() with very large shared_buffers, and parallel worker launch floods go undetected.
brief.proposed_design: The postmaster checks its counters and getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) once per second. It logs a stats line when it used more than 75% of one CPU core, ran late, or could not serve a connection, or when new connections per second exceed a set threshold. The design moved from v1 periodic logging (log_postmaster_stats) to threshold-based logging after Robert Haas's review.
user_visible_surface: GUC log_postmaster_overloads (boolean, default off, postgresql.conf or command line only).
GUC log_postmaster_excess_connections (integer connections/sec, default 0 = disabled, postgresql.conf or command line only).

LOG messages "postmaster potentially overloaded, stats: ..." and "postmaster excessive connections, stats: ..." with conns, disconns, conn errors and parallel workers per second, plus CPU user/system/elapsed.
author_claims: A storm of about 1800 connections/sec costs the postmaster about 5 s of system CPU per 10 s.
Under 200 to 300 connections/sec can already drive the postmaster to 100% system CPU on some setups.
getrusage() once per second costs nothing measurable next to thousands of fork() calls per second.
A raw connection-rate threshold is hard to choose, so the CPU-based switch is the main feature.
Postmaster bottlenecks occur in the field, and the author cites earlier threads and new cases.
brief.thread_state: Robert Haas objected to the log-based design, then supported emergency logging but asked to drop the CPU checks and keep only a connection-rate threshold. The author kept both GUCs in v3 and v4, Robert has not answered, and the duplicate log lines when both GUCs are on are still open.
unclear: Whether Robert Haas or any other reviewer accepts keeping the CPU-based GUC after his objection.
The material does not define "getting late on CPU" or how much delay triggers a message.
The CPU test is mostly commented out because CI cannot overload the postmaster, so the proposal has no reliable test for it.
The proposal does not say how messages are throttled during a long storm, beyond one line per second.
The proposal does not say why the 75% threshold is fixed and not configurable.

objections.title: CPU-based trigger kept against reviewer advice and cannot be tested
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes the postmaster wait loop or the timing of its wakeups. The log_postmaster_overloads path then stops firing, or fires on every disk stall, and no test fails because the CPU test is commented out. Users find out during an incident, when the expected message is missing or misleading.
objections.argument: Robert asked in message #7 to drop the CPU checks and keep only a connection-rate threshold, partly so the test could pass reliably. In message #8 the author kept both GUCs, citing the difficulty of choosing a rate. Message #6 says CI cannot overload the postmaster, and the commit message defines overload as "75% or getting late on CPU" without saying what "late" means. Robert has not replied since v3, so no committer has accepted owning an untested, scheduler-dependent trigger.
objections.author_must_show: Can log_postmaster_overloads be split into a separate later patch, after log_postmaster_excess_connections is committed with its reliable test?

critic.reasoning: Message #6 confirms that CI cannot overload the postmaster and that the CPU test is mostly commented out. A trigger that depends on scheduling and has no test can break without any failure, which is a design-level maintainability concern.

objections.title: Boolean overload GUC hides a fixed 75% CPU rule and an undefined lateness rule
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA enables log_postmaster_overloads and gets "potentially overloaded" lines while the postmaster waits on a slow disk or network write. On another machine a heavy storm uses only 60% of a fast core and nothing is logged. The DBA cannot tune either case because the trigger is hard-coded.
objections.argument: The commit message defines overload as "75% or getting late on CPU" but does not say how late counts as late. In message #7 Robert Haas predicted these false positives and false negatives and asked to drop the CPU checks. Message #8 keeps them as the "main feature" and gives no answer on misfires, so a committer would likely see the open point as unsettled. Once the GUC ships, its meaning becomes part of the contract, and changing the 75% rule or the lateness rule later changes behaviour for existing users.
objections.author_must_show: What exact condition triggers log_postmaster_overloads, and why should 75% and the lateness rule be fixed and not settable?

critic.reasoning: The v4 docs state the 75% rule but do not define "getting late on CPU". Message #8 answers the cost of getrusage() but not the false positives and false negatives raised in message #7.

objections.title: Two GUCs log the same stats twice per second during a storm
objections.failure_scenario: A site sets both log_postmaster_overloads = on and log_postmaster_excess_connections = 200. During a long connection storm the postmaster writes two lines with the same numbers every second, so the log doubles at the moment it is already under load. Log-based alert rules that count lines double their counts.
objections.argument: Message #9 shows the duplicate output and leaves the fix open. Both settings guard one diagnostic, with two triggers and two names, where Postgres usually has one parameter per diagnostic. The proposal also has no limit on lines per storm beyond one per second, so a storm that lasts an hour writes thousands of lines.
objections.author_must_show: Why does one diagnostic need two independent GUCs, and what does the log contain when both trigger in the same second?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 shows the duplicate lines and offers a merged message only as an idea, so v4 still emits both. A new patch version can fix this.

objections.title: The name log_postmaster_excess_connections does not say it is a rate
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA reads the name next to max_connections, takes it as a count of open sessions, and sets it to 500. The setting means 500 new connections per second, so a real storm of 300 per second is never logged.
objections.argument: In message #7 Robert Haas proposed log_excessive_connection_rate because that name tells users what the setting means. The v4 name drops "rate", and the integer has no unit, while nearby connection settings count sessions. Message #8 argues that a raw rate is hard to choose but does not explain the name.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a name without "rate" or a per-second unit better than the log_excessive_connection_rate spelling suggested in message #7?

critic.reasoning: The docs say the value is connections per second, but the name does not, and message #7 asked for a name that explains itself. The thread gives no reason for dropping "rate".

objections.title: Postmaster CPU checks duplicate per-process OS monitoring
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA turns on log_postmaster_overloads and also runs a host agent that samples per-process CPU, or pidstat on the PID from postmaster.pid. Both report the same saturation, but the core check uses a fixed 75% threshold and a one-second window the DBA cannot tune. The server log then carries a second, less flexible copy of data the OS already records.
objections.argument: Per-process CPU history of the postmaster is available today from standard OS tools, sampled at any interval, with the PID taken from postmaster.pid. Message #5 says the real problem is that users miss one busy core among many busy backends, which makes the OS route less visible but still possible. Robert Haas (message #7) supported a connection-rate threshold and asked to drop the CPU checks; log_postmaster_excess_connections covers what core alone can see. The 75% CPU switch mostly repeats OS accounting inside the postmaster loop.
objections.author_must_show: Which postmaster overload cases does the CPU check catch that log_postmaster_excess_connections and per-process OS CPU sampling of the postmaster PID both miss?

critic.reasoning: OS per-process sampling can record postmaster CPU, and the thread's only answer is that users overlook it on large hosts. The material does not show a case that both the rate GUC and OS sampling miss.

refuted.title: Per-process overload GUCs do not pass the accumulation test
refuted.failure_scenario: The same reasoning applies to the checkpointer, bgwriter, walsender and startup process, which message #5 also names. Each would get its own boolean GUC, its own hard-coded 75% threshold, and its own log format. Ten of these give users a set of special-case switches and no single place to look.
refuted.argument: Message #5 says the real gap is the lack of a way to see single-core saturation of single-threaded subsystems, and it lists five of them. The patch solves this for one process only, with a fixed threshold built in. A committer would likely ask for one shape that the other processes could reuse later, for example a shared helper or a per-process rusage counter in cumulative statistics, which message #4 named as the usual practice.
refuted.author_must_show: How would the same overload detection be extended to the checkpointer or walsender without adding a new GUC and log format for each one?

critic.reasoning: Nobody in the thread proposes the same GUC for other processes, so the scenario is hypothetical. Per-process log settings such as log_checkpoints and log_startup_progress_interval are existing practice, and message #7 calls threshold logging "a good direction".

refuted.title: Demand for the CPU-based trigger rests on the author's own cases
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer accepts both GUCs, and log_postmaster_overloads becomes a second, CPU-based trigger that few sites turn on. Its behaviour is hard to test in CI and hard to explain, so it stays in the docs while sites that need the data keep using OS process monitoring.
refuted.argument: Message #7 found the connection-rate trigger desirable and asked to drop the CPU checks. The field evidence that only the CPU trigger catches is the author's 512GB shared_buffers fork() case on older kernels (message #5), one more link (message #8) and an unnamed case (message #9). The PQ-worker report quoted in message #5 is a connection-rate storm, which log_postmaster_excess_connections already detects. Per-process CPU sampling with pidstat or a host agent exists today, and the author's answer is that DBAs miss it on 128-vCPU hosts.
refuted.author_must_show: Which field cases, from users other than the author, saturated the postmaster without a connection or worker rate that log_postmaster_excess_connections would have flagged?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which asks the same question about cases only the CPU trigger catches. The title also overstates: the reports linked in messages #5 and #8 are other threads, which the author presents as field cases.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds log_postmaster_overloads and log_postmaster_excess_connections.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Unauthenticated connection attempts can trigger the new LOG lines, at about one line per second per GUC.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The CPU trigger depends on postmaster loop timing and its test is mostly commented out.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The postmaster main loop gains counters and a once-per-second getrusage() check when a GUC is on.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The 75% CPU check overlaps per-process CPU sampling that OS tools already provide.

questions: Which postmaster overload cases does the CPU check catch that log_postmaster_excess_connections and OS sampling of the postmaster PID both miss?
What exact delay counts as "getting late on CPU", and why are that rule and the 75% threshold fixed?
Can log_postmaster_overloads move to a separate later patch, so log_postmaster_excess_connections can be committed first with its reliable test?
What does the log contain when both GUCs trigger in the same second, and is there any limit during an hour-long storm?
Why is log_postmaster_excess_connections preferred over the log_excessive_connection_rate name suggested in message #7?

committability.owner_note: Robert Haas reviewed up to message #7 but has not answered v3 or v4. The owner needs to know the postmaster main loop and its wakeup timing.
committability.liability: Two GUC names, a log line format that alert rules will parse, and the fixed 75% and lateness rules, all for as long as the GUCs exist. The CPU trigger has no working test.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted four versions between May and message #9 and moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October 2026.

priority.reason: Sites with connection storms gain from the rate threshold, and the patch is about 24 KiB, mostly in postmaster.c. The open disagreement about the CPU trigger blocks progress more than patch size does.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check how the lateness rule is computed, where the counters sit in the connection accept path, or what the TAP test covers. Only 3 of 9 messages were shown in full.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use SIGIO to detect postmaster death
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses SIGIO, set up with fcntl(O_ASYNC) and F_SETOWN on the postmaster death pipe, so backends get a signal when the postmaster exits. This gives a postmaster death signal on systems without USE_POSTMASTER_DEATH_SIGNAL, such as macOS and the BSDs.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after finding that only the last backend to call F_SETOWN on the shared pipe receives the signal. A fix would need a separate pipe per backend, which he judged unwarranted at that point. Heikki Linnakangas and Tom Lane had reviewed it without objection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
On closer inspection, only the last backend to start up and do
F_SETOWN on the pipe receives the signal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Create a new session for postmaster in pg_ctl
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made the postmaster call setsid() so it leaves the controlling terminal's session, which stops a Ctrl-C in the starting shell from killing the server. After Tom Lane's review, the author moved the setsid() call into pg_ctl start.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier objected that the pg_ctl version breaks a development workflow: Ctrl-C on pg_ctl during recovery no longer stops the started instance. He asked for an opt-in switch with the current behavior as default, while Tom Lane preferred detaching by default and suggested a postmaster switch that pg_ctl passes. Andres Freund opposed the postmaster daemonizing itself, and the patch was returned with feedback for an optional pg_ctl-based approach.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I would be ready to
accept a patch which does not change the default behavior, and makes the
deamonization behavior activated only if an option switch is given by
the user, like -d/--daemon.  So I am -1 for what is proposed in its
current shape.

precedents_retrieved.title: Enable fine-grained control over what gets logged on connection attempt (reduces log size)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a list-valued GUC (later named log_connection_messages) that selects which connection stages get logged: received, authenticated, authorized, disconnected, or all. It replaces log_connections and log_disconnections, so sites with many short-lived connections can drop redundant log lines.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The fourth version of the patch failed the ldap_password_func test on all platforms because pg_ctl could not start, and the reviewer set the entry to Waiting on Author. The author sent no fixed version, so the patch was returned with feedback for failing tests and a stalled thread. No reviewer objected to the design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With the patch failing tests and the thread stalled with no update I am marking
this returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Do not exit on postmaster death event inside CRIT sections.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes a process that detects postmaster death inside WaitEventSetWait defer its exit while it is in a critical section, and exit only after the section ends. The goal was to stop proc_exit(1) from releasing LWLocks mid-change, which let the checkpointer flush a modified buffer whose WAL record was never written.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that deferring exit leads to systems that fail to shut down. The author then confirmed that the checkpointer waits forever in LWLockAcquire in the test. Tom also argued that proc_exit(1) after postmaster death is the real defect, and that removing the death check is as hazardous as keeping it this late in the v18 cycle. The thread instead reverted commit bc22dc0e0, which had started using condition variables inside critical sections, and left better postmaster-death handling to a new thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I do not like this patch one bit: it will replace one set of problems with another set, namely systems that fail to shut down.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid possibly slow processing during postmaster abnormal or immediate shutdown
precedents_retrieved.summary: Two patches to shorten postmaster shutdown after a backend crash or an immediate shutdown. One makes the stats collector exit on SIGQUIT without writing the stats files, and the other closes the listening sockets as soon as the postmaster knows it will stop all children and exit.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that commit 82233ce7e in 9.4 already solves the problem better, because the postmaster now sends SIGKILL to child processes after 5 seconds during a crash or immediate shutdown. The original complaint was against 9.2. Peter Eisentraut agreed, and he also objected that early socket close stops PQping() and error-message monitoring and makes the crash and immediate modes behave differently from the other shutdown modes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
My feeling is that 82233ce7e has obsoleted all of the proposals made so
far in this thread, and that we should reject them all.

This reverts commit 88bdbd3f746049834ae3cc972e6e650586ec3c9d.

As committed, statement sampling used the existing duration threshold
(log_min_duration_statement) when decide which statements to sample.
The issue is that even the longest statements are subject to sampling,
and so may not end up logged. An improvement was proposed, introducing

precedents_retrieved.title: allow to set log_statement_sample_limit - maximal duration for sampling
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a GUC log_statement_sample_limit so that statements running longer than it are always logged, which turns off log_statement_sample_rate sampling for them. Below the limit, statements over log_min_duration_statement would still be sampled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra found that the three settings were confusing, because log_min_duration_statement acted as a minimum and the new limit acted as a maximum. He proposed two minimum thresholds instead, with a new log_min_duration_sample for sampling and log_min_duration_statement logging everything above it. He reverted log_statement_sample_rate from v12 and later pushed that reworked design, which made this patch unnecessary.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
IMO that's bound to be confusing for users, because one threshold
behaves as minimum while the other behaves as maximum.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add sample rate to auto_explain
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a sample rate setting to auto_explain so that it explains, and optionally analyzes, only a share of queries, which lowers the cost of EXPLAIN ANALYZE logging. The patch uses a per-backend counter that starts at a random value and does not count nested statements.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund asked for random sampling per query instead of the counter, because queries issued in a fixed pattern could be sampled only in part. He also asked for the rate as a fraction between 0 and 1. Julien Rouhaud repeated both points in his review, but no revised patch addressed them, and Craig Ringer said he had no time to return to it. Michael Paquier then marked the entry returned with feedback without stating a further reason.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Wouldn't random sampling be better than what you do? If your queries
have a pattern to them (e.g. you always issue the same 10 queries in
succession), this will possibly only show a subset of the queries.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve logicalrep_worker_launch() logic
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes logicalrep_worker_launch() so it also runs garbage collection of worker slots when the per-subscription parallel apply worker limit is reached, as it already does for the sync worker limit. It also reuses the slot that garbage collection just freed, instead of scanning all worker slots again.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila argued that the parallel apply case is not a clear bug, because the apply worker applies changes itself when no parallel apply worker is available. He asked for a test case that reproduces the problem rather than a change based on reading the code. The thread ends with that request unanswered, and the entry was withdrawn about eight months later. No message states the reason for the withdrawal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
No, the idea was that if we are changing the code, it is better to
test it via a testcase instead of changing based on assumptions.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P3] changed which connection stages log_connections reports and was returned because its tests failed and the thread stalled, so neither its idea nor its reason applies here. Messages #5 and #8 link earlier threads, but only as field reports of postmaster bottlenecks, not as earlier attempts at this feature.
Robert Haas raised the cumulative-statistics concern in message #4. He supported the emergency-logging direction in message #7, so it is not raised here.

The proposal adds two postmaster-only GUCs, in-memory counters and LOG lines, with no on-disk format, WAL, catalog, protocol or replication state to check. The change to bgworker_internals.h is an internal header, not a documented extension API, so this angle finds no persistent or cross-node concern.

No security objection. Both GUCs can be set only in postgresql.conf or on the command line, and both are off by default. The messages hold aggregate counts and postmaster CPU times, with no user, database or query data. Unauthenticated clients can trigger the lines, but output is capped at about one line per second per GUC, which is much less than log_connections writes today. Without the code I could not check that the counters and getrusage() add nothing that an unauthenticated client can exploit.
Hot-path cost is not raised. Both GUCs default to off, and the once-per-second check falls only on users who turn them on.

The connection-rate threshold has no equivalent in core: pg_stat_database.sessions keeps no per-second history, and log_connections costs too much to leave on. Robert Haas endorsed that part in message #7, so this angle raises nothing against it.

The connection-rate GUC has credible demand. The author reports field cases, cites a thread with 2000 to 3000 connect requests per minute from parallel workers (message #5), and Robert Haas supported emergency logging in message #7. Both GUCs are off by default, so only users of the feature pay. The objection covers only the CPU-based GUC.
